title: The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Control in a Distributed Problem Solver
authors: Reid G. Smith
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computers, vol. C-29, no. 12, pp. 1104-1113

summary: Addresses how a network of loosely coupled problem-solving nodes can distribute tasks among themselves without central control. The paper presents the message types and negotiation structure as a general high-level communication and control mechanism for distributed problem solvers.
relevance: The canonical announce-bid-award delegation protocol that modern agent-to-agent task handoff (e.g. A2A task negotiation) implicitly re-creates.

authors: Butler Lampson; Martín Abadi; Michael Burrows; Edward Wobber

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

summary: The paper argues that once LLM applications retrieve external content, the boundary between data and instructions disappears, so an attacker can plant prompts in data the model will later read without ever talking to it directly. summary: Mem0 is a memory layer for LLM agents that extracts the salient facts from ongoing multi-session conversations, consolidates them and retrieves them later; a variant stores memories as a graph to capture relations between entities. title: Here Comes the AI Worm: Preventing the Propagation of Adversarial Self-Replicating Prompts Within GenAI Ecosystems

summary: The paper shows that when GenAI-powered applications exchange messages and rely on RAG-based inference, an adversarial self-replicating prompt can start a worm-like chain of indirect prompt injections, called RAGworm, in which each compromised application acts maliciously and contaminates the retrieval stores of other applications. title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design

summary: CaMeL wraps an LLM agent in a protective system layer so that it stays secure even if the underlying model is susceptible to prompt injection. summary: The paper shows that checkpoint-restore in LLM agent frameworks is unsafe because, after a restore, an agent re-generates tool requests that differ slightly from the originals, so servers treat them as new. summary: The paper shows that prompt injection can spread between LLM agents in a multi-agent system: an injected prompt copies itself from agent to agent, so the attack moves through the system like a computer virus.
